title: I Buried Sid

jokes.text: Stand-up bit about complaining and the post office — 'a penny every 11 years... 32 cents. Whoo-ooh-ooh...'
jokes.setup: Larry riffs on how Americans love to complain, using stamps as an example of hollow grievances
jokes.punchline: The exaggerated mock-outrage at 32 cents — 'Whoo-ooh-ooh' — deflates the complaint by exposing how trivial it is
jokes.explanation: Competent observational stand-up but very mid-90s and generic. The bit works on a surface level — the self-aware exaggeration of the outrage is mildly funny — but it's not character-specific to Larry and wouldn't be out of place in any club act of the era. Functional stage-setting material.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, but what, like a penny every 11 years? I mean, what is it... what is it now, 32 cents. Whoo-ooh-ooh... is it 32 cents? That sounds high.

jokes.text: 'Is it 32 cents? That sounds high.' — Larry breaks mid-set to genuinely question his own material
jokes.setup: Larry delivers the 32-cents punchline with mock outrage as if it's polished material
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it by sincerely doubting the factual accuracy of his own joke mid-performance
jokes.explanation: This is the meta-joke inside the stand-up bit that actually works: Larry, the insecure host who can't let anything go without second-guessing himself, breaks his own routine to wonder if his premise is even correct. It's perfectly character-integrated — this IS Larry Sanders — and economical to the point of genius. Six words that tell you everything about his vanity and anxiety.

dialogue.line: You're a funny guy.

jokes.text: 'Sounds captivating.' — Larry's dry response when his secret girlfriend says she spent the night alone
jokes.setup: Laura asks what Larry did last night; he claims he was home alone. She asks follow-up, implying she expected him to be with her
jokes.punchline: 'Sounds captivating' — delivered with zero affect, puncturing any romantic warmth in the scene
jokes.explanation: A clean Larry-as-Larry moment: he's checking whether she was alone (jealousy, insecurity) and then when she confirms it, deflects with bored sarcasm rather than revealing genuine feeling. The economy is excellent. Works because it fits the character's emotional avoidance pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: when celebrity relationships go public, and... I don't know. It starts to ruin everything.

jokes.text: Rehearsal: Liza Minnelli bursts out singing 'Cabaret' and cannot be stopped
jokes.setup: Hank rehearses introducing Liza Minnelli as a farewell guest. Liza is supposed to say a few words.
jokes.punchline: Liza launches into full-throated 'Cabaret' with no signs of stopping, overrunning the segment entirely
jokes.explanation: The joke is that the show within the show can't control its own guest even in rehearsal. The escalation of Liza singing through all attempts to stop her is the engine of a running gag that pays off later.

dialogue.line: Sounds captivating.

jokes.text: 'OK. Sorry... sorry. Thank you, liza.' / 'I'm sorry. I was supposed to interrupt sooner.' — The whole production fumbles its own rehearsal
jokes.setup: Larry is supposed to interrupt Liza mid-song but missed his cue
jokes.punchline: Sid apologizes — it was his fault for not cueing Larry — exposing that the show's behind-the-scenes coordination is as chaotic as it looks on-air
jokes.explanation: Small but precise — the comedy of a show-within-a-show screwing up its own scripted bit in rehearsal. The meta-layer (a scripted mess-up about a scripted moment) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Sid as Liza Minnelli
dialogue.line: Screw you, Larry! My mother and I always hated you!

jokes.text: 'Screw you, Larry! My mother and I always hated you!'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to politely interrupt Liza with 'That's enough, liza. One number is fine.' — a diplomatic, professional request
jokes.punchline: Liza drops all pretense of celebrity decorum and explodes with the deeply personal 'My mother and I always hated you!'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and surprise. The specificity of 'My mother and I' — invoking Judy Garland as the silent co-hater — is the genius detail. It's not just an insult, it's a multi-generational, celebrity-gossip-inflected insult that only lands in this exact context. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific (only a Liza bit would have this layer), and structurally perfect: the politest possible request met with the most nuclear personal rejection.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tour de force. New face in town, Sid. Hilarious.

jokes.text: Liza continues singing through multiple attempts to stop her, then Sid comments 'Tour de force. New face in town, Sid.'
jokes.setup: Everyone tries to stop Liza from singing; she keeps going verse after verse
jokes.punchline: Sid's dry 'Tour de force. New face in town' — praising a disastrous, unstoppable performance with sycophantic showbiz language
jokes.explanation: Sid's industry-speak deflection — reframing chaos as artistic triumph — is a precise skewering of Hollywood sycophancy. 'New face in town' is an absurdist flourish given that this IS Liza Minnelli. The economy of the praise-as-deflection gag is very sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It means that you're a fucking freak.

jokes.text: 'They wanted a freak show, and you gave it to 'em.' / 'What's that supposed to mean?' / 'It means that you're a fucking freak.'
jokes.setup: Someone offers what sounds like a backhanded compliment after Hank's performance
jokes.punchline: The explicit clarification — 'It means that you're a fucking freak' — removes all ambiguity with blunt brutality
jokes.explanation: The structure is a classic misdirection: a phrase that could mean two things, followed by ruthless disambiguation. The profanity lands because it's calibrated — this isn't random aggression, it's specific cruelty. Good economy; the exchange is four lines and fully complete.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You don't know the fucking difference between being laughed with and being laughed at.

jokes.text: 'You don't know the fucking difference between being laughed with and being laughed at.'
jokes.setup: Hank is defending his Liza performance; the crew member has been insulting him throughout
jokes.punchline: The philosophical gut-punch — invoking the classic comedy distinction to destroy Hank — lands with devastating specificity
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: it's a precise insult, AND it plants the episode's thematic seed — this exact phrase will be weaponized by Larry against Sid and then echoed at the end. The show's writers are doing something clever: the same words that destroy Hank here will later haunt Larry. High rewatch value for this reason.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He said, 'is there a man in your life with a 'd' and an 'a' and a 'd?' I said, 'yeah, that's my dad.'

jokes.text: 'We leave that and teenage makeovers to Ms. Ricki Lake.'
jokes.setup: Beverly pitches a psychic for the show; Artie dismisses it
jokes.punchline: Artie's dismissal isn't just 'no' — it's a specific, hierarchical industry dig placing psychics and makeovers in the Ricki Lake tier, below their show
jokes.explanation: Very Artie: institutional pride and snobbery wrapped in a casual insult. The specificity of 'Ms. Ricki Lake' (the formal honorific making it more cutting) is excellent character work. Artie's TV-hierarchy worldview is crystallized in one line.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: On most nights, you'd be batting 1,000.

jokes.text: Artie dismisses the psychic idea by saying 'We leave that and teenage makeovers to Ms. Ricki Lake.'
jokes.setup: A staff member (Beverly?) is pushing Artie to book a psychic on the show
jokes.punchline: Artie categorizes psychics and 'teenage makeovers' as Ricki Lake territory — an insider showbiz burn that establishes the show's highbrow self-image
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie — dismissive, hierarchical, expressed through a sharp industry-insider reference. The Ricki Lake namecheck is perfectly calibrated (not too obscure, not too obvious). Economy is excellent. Deeply in Artie's character voice: the old-school TV producer who knows where the cultural lines are drawn.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Is there also an 'h,' and an 'r,' char?

jokes.text: Kreskin's 'Is there a man in your life with a D and an A and a D?' / 'Yeah, that's my dad.'
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining why psychics don't impress him, citing Kreskin trying the grandma trick on him 20 years ago
jokes.punchline: The D-A-D spelling trick — so transparent that 'dad' is the only possible answer — is the oldest cold-reading con, and Artie saw through it immediately
jokes.explanation: Artie demonstrates the psychic trick by performing it, which is inherently funny — he becomes Kreskin in the retelling. The D-A-D example is perfectly chosen because it's so obvious it exposes the entire enterprise. Rip Torn's delivery would milk every syllable. Sharp and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: You have the worse handwriting than stephen hawking.

jokes.text: 'I see a new woman in your life.' / 'On most nights, you'd be batting 1,000.'
jokes.setup: Char opens with a cold-reading gambit about a 'new woman' — clearly a statistical guess
jokes.punchline: Artie's response admits she's probably right statistically while simultaneously refusing to be impressed — 'most nights' implying his romantic life is chaotic enough that a new woman is nearly always present
jokes.explanation: Artie in one line: debunks the psychic, implies a libertine lifestyle, and does it with pure deadpan. 'On most nights, you'd be batting 1,000' is a very quotable, very Rip Torn line. Perfect character integration — only an Artie character says this.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Good for you. You gotta set an example. No. I mean, he killed himself.

jokes.text: 'Your mother, did she have dark hair, and was there an A in her name?' / 'How did you know that?' / 'Adele?' / 'See?'
jokes.setup: Char deploys the 'A in the name' cold-reading trick — a statistical near-certainty given how common A names are
jokes.punchline: Artie genuinely falls for it ('How did you know that?'), having just spent 30 seconds explaining why he can't be fooled by psychics
jokes.explanation: The callback makes this: Artie just finished explaining exactly how the D-A-D trick works, and then immediately falls for the exact same trick with 'A in the name.' The irony is structurally tight and character-appropriate — Artie's gruff confidence is his blind spot. Beverly's triumphant 'See?' is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Some nights you have such special... special show where you have terrific guests, and some nights, honestly, you just have, you know, average guests. But tonight's one of those nights where we have... have really good guests.

jokes.text: Char says 'And you had a grandfather named jacob.' Artie: 'Grandpa Jake. Taught me how to fish.'
jokes.setup: Char is running her cold reading; Artie has been getting progressively more credulous
jokes.punchline: Artie doesn't just confirm — he adds a nostalgic detail ('Taught me how to fish') that reveals how completely he's been sucked in. The warmth of the detail is funny.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in how quickly and completely Artie has been converted — going from hardened skeptic to emotionally reminiscing about fishing with Grandpa Jake in about 30 seconds. The specificity of 'Taught me how to fish' is charming and grounds Artie as a real person while also making him look ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I wonder if they'll ask me to be a pallbearer? Because, you know, I have a bad... back? Shoulder?

jokes.text: 'Is there also an H, and an R, char?' — Artie realizes the psychic's letters spell her own name
jokes.setup: Char is spelling out letters for the 'new woman': C... A... — building suspense about who it might be
jokes.punchline: Artie flatly completes the name — C-H-A-R — exposing that she's basically describing herself
jokes.explanation: Artie's deadpan completion of the psychic's own name is tightly constructed and very funny. The question format — 'Is there also an H, and an R, char?' — adds a mock-psychic quality to Artie's debunking, making him do the trick back at her. Economy is exceptional: six words that simultaneously puncture the illusion and get the laugh. One of the episode's cleanest jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I told him he was a... a... a fourth rate Larry bud melman.

jokes.text: 'I predict a booking on Friday night.' — Artie offers the psychic a booking to get rid of her
jokes.setup: Artie has just thoroughly debunked Char's psychic routine
jokes.punchline: He offers her a booking anyway — using her own 'prediction' language — which is the exact opposite of what he just argued the show should do
jokes.explanation: Artie's practical TV-producer instincts override his principles in real time. The mirroring of her 'prediction' language is a nice touch. Very Artie — he's a showman first, a snob second.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Call rosie grier. Ask him if he'll come over and pray with me.

jokes.text: 'Goddamn it, where is that little asshole?' — Phil's outburst about Sid being late, immediately before learning Sid is dead
jokes.setup: Phil is furious about Sid's absence 5 minutes before the show, cursing him out
jokes.punchline: The audience (and Artie) know what Phil doesn't: Sid has just killed himself. Phil's profane rage is horrifically misplaced.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is situational: Phil is righteously furious at a dead man. The joke lives entirely in context and dramatic irony, and it lands because the show trusts the audience to hold both the comedy and the horror simultaneously. A lesser show would soften Phil's anger; this one lets him fully commit to it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: cue card men never die. They just get whited out.

jokes.text: 'You have worse handwriting than Stephen Hawking.' — Phil to Brian
jokes.setup: Phil is scrambling for someone to write cue cards with Sid absent
jokes.punchline: The Stephen Hawking comparison — evoking the wheelchair-bound physicist who communicates through a speech synthesizer — is an absurdly dark insult about handwriting
jokes.explanation: Edgy, mildly lazy — the Hawking comparison is unexpected enough to get a laugh but doesn't fully earn it. Still, in the context of Phil's mounting panic it works as escalating chaos comedy. Mid-tier.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No flipping. Shut up, Phil.

jokes.text: 'He's dead. There ya go. Good for you. You gotta set an example. No. I mean, he killed himself.'
jokes.setup: Artie tells everyone Sid isn't there; a crew member says 'I think you gotta take some action, people have been fired for a lot less'
jokes.punchline: Artie says 'He's dead' — the crew member, not registering it, says 'Good for you, you gotta set an example' — then Artie clarifies: 'No. I mean, he killed himself.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The crew member's 'Good for you' — treating 'he's dead' as a firing metaphor — is a perfect comic misunderstanding rooted in TV-production tunnel vision. The show-must-go-on mentality is so ingrained that the word 'dead' doesn't even register as literal. The beat where the clarification lands ('No. I mean, he killed himself') is devastating and hilarious simultaneously. This is the show at its best: the comedy of dehumanizing institutional momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It didn't work, but you know why? Because you went so long. You know, you killed the whole audience.

jokes.text: 'Well, we've got exactly 4 minutes. Gotta do a show. Let's do this one for Sid. What do you say? And not a word of this to Larry.'
jokes.setup: The staff has just learned Sid killed himself
jokes.punchline: Artie's response is a locker-room pep talk — 'do this one for Sid' — immediately followed by the show-must-go-on command to keep it from the talent
jokes.explanation: Artie at peak Artie: the sports-movie 'do this one for Sid' speech delivered with complete sincerity, then immediately followed by the utterly unsentimental 'not a word to Larry' — because the show's functioning matters more than anyone's grief, including the host's. The whiplash between genuine feeling and producer pragmatism is quintessential Artie and couldn't be anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A very gifted actor who people laughed with and not at.

jokes.text: Larry struggles to introduce guests on air — 'We have a great show tonight... some nights you have such special show... tonight's one of those nights where we have... have really good guests.'
jokes.setup: Larry doesn't know Sid is dead and is improvising without cue cards, clearly flustered
jokes.punchline: The monologue dissolves into a word-salad of tautologies ('great show... special show... really good guests') with no actual content — he literally can't say what the guests are
jokes.explanation: The joke of a professional broadcaster reduced to pure filler when his crutch is gone. The repetition of 'great/special/really good' with no information is a pitch-perfect portrait of on-air panic dressed in host-speak. Character-specific to Larry's reliance on the machinery around him.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Um, you know, snaps.

jokes.text: 'Who died?' / 'Sid. He killed himself this afternoon.'
jokes.setup: Larry has clearly sensed something is off backstage after the show
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Who died?' is asked as a rhetorical expression of something being wrong; Artie answers it literally
jokes.explanation: The classic 'idiom answered literally' structure, but elevated by the gravity of what's being revealed. Larry asking 'who died?' as a figure of speech and being told the actual answer is a genuine tragicomic gut-punch. The joke is in the collision of register.

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Got a lot of unpaid bills, and, uh, insurance policy, borrowed money, and I'd like to help, but I'm living on unemployment...

jokes.text: The Larry-Artie post-show logistics exchange: send flowers — done. Funeral — tomorrow afternoon. Appearance — 20 minutes, car will be waiting.
jokes.setup: Larry is processing that his cue-card holder has died; he and Artie start planning
jokes.punchline: Every emotional impulse Larry has is instantly pre-solved by Artie before Larry even finishes the sentence — reducing grief to logistics
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. Artie has already handled everything — flowers, funeral, car — because he knows Larry's grief will be performative and time-bounded. The rhythm is perfect: Larry begins an emotional sentence, Artie cuts it off with the logistical answer already completed. 'Short appearance. 20 minutes, tops. Car will be waiting.' is devastating in its efficiency. This exchange perfectly encapsulates the Larry-Artie dynamic: Artie is Larry's emotional handler as much as his producer. High rewatch bonus because it recontextualizes everything we know about both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: because I loved him.

jokes.text: 'I wonder if they'll ask me to be a pallbearer? Because, you know, I have a bad... back? Shoulder?'
jokes.setup: Larry is in the middle of processing Sid's death; he starts worrying about pallbearer duties
jokes.punchline: He's already preparing his excuse for not doing it — and doesn't even know what injury to cite — revealing that his primary concern about Sid's funeral is his own inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Larry Sanders: he invents a fake injury before he's even been asked, and he can't keep the fake injury straight ('back? Shoulder?'). The joke works because it's so specifically Larry — self-centered, conflict-avoidant, and doing a lazy job of hiding it. The uncertainty between 'back' and 'shoulder' is the perfect button that exposes the lie in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Fake things. I mean, you know... oh. Fake dinosaurs.

jokes.text: 'I'm going to hell.' / 'I killed Sid.'
jokes.setup: Larry processes the news of Sid's death and what he said to him at rehearsal
jokes.punchline: Larry concludes he personally killed Sid — the narcissistic leap that makes his guilt about himself rather than about Sid
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's simultaneously true (the words were cruel) and narcissistically overblown (Sid had a whole life — a dead wife, a girlfriend, debt — that had nothing to do with Larry). Larry centering himself in Sid's death is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wasn't it at a function where I don't remember you?

jokes.text: 'Call Rosie Grier. Ask him if he'll come over and pray with me.'
jokes.setup: Larry is spiraling with guilt and says he needs someone to pray with him
jokes.punchline: The specific choice of Rosie Grier — former NFL defensive lineman turned motivational Christian speaker — is so oddly specific it becomes genuinely funny; then: 'He's a good guy, right?' / 'Mm-hmm, and very discreet.'
jokes.explanation: The celebrity-as-spiritual-resource gag is very Larry — he can't just call a pastor, it has to be a famous person. The addition of 'and very discreet' is Artie treating a prayer meeting like a crisis PR situation. Very funny industry-brain moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Fuck me.

jokes.text: Eulogy reaction beat: the crowd's long, reverent silence after 'That was the essence of Sid' — cut to Larry leaning over to Hank: 'That was long.'
jokes.setup: A heartfelt eulogy is delivered about Sid being a 'real hero'
jokes.punchline: Larry's only takeaway is that it ran long — he immediately pivots to stage management at a funeral
jokes.explanation: Larry timing a eulogy like a talk show segment is perfect character comedy. 'That was long' at a funeral — delivered as a professional note, not a complaint — is Larry's inability to leave the show behind even for a moment. Economy is perfect: two words that say everything.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Uh, does anybody take discover anymore? I mean, was this guy current on anything?

jokes.text: 'Introduce me. Introduce me.' / Larry introduces Hank as 'one of Sid's biggest fans'
jokes.setup: Hank wants Larry to introduce him to the crowd at the funeral
jokes.punchline: Larry introduces him as 'one of Sid's biggest fans' — Hank who despised Sid — which is either oblivious or Larry subtly trolling him
jokes.explanation: The irony of calling Hank Sid's 'biggest fan' — when they actively disliked each other — works on the show's insider-knowledge level. Hank wanting to be introduced at a funeral (at all) is also a great Hank-is-always-performing moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What did you say to Sid? When? Right after rehearsal when you walked away from me and made a beeline backstage, probably to tell him how rotten he was and how much better you'd be in the sketch, right?

jokes.text: Larry's funeral speech: '...the most important part of the show, and the funniest. Anyway, just a real loss, but cue card men never die. They just get whited out.'
jokes.setup: Larry is delivering what's supposed to be a heartfelt tribute to Sid at his own funeral
jokes.punchline: He pivots from promoting his own monologue ('the most important, the funniest') to a cue card pun — 'They just get whited out' — at the graveside
jokes.explanation: The episode's peak joke. Larry's funeral eulogy becomes a self-promotion (calling his monologue 'the most important, the funniest'), then lands on a pun so specific to Sid's job ('whited out') that it's simultaneously the most appropriate thing anyone could say AND the most inappropriate. The pun is earned — it actually works as a sendoff AND as a pun — which is rare. The setup (Larry can't stop being a host even at a funeral) perfectly earns the punchline. High quotability, very high craft. 'Cue card men never die, they just get whited out' is the kind of line that gets repeated.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We... we never got to that.

jokes.text: 'Cue card men never die. They just get whited out.'
jokes.setup: Larry, having rambled about himself, finally attempts a tribute line about Sid's profession.
jokes.punchline: 'They just get whited out.' — a cue-card joke at a funeral for someone who died by suicide is an astonishing swing.
jokes.explanation: The pun works on a technical level (white-out is used to correct cue cards; Sid is being 'erased' by death), and the audacity of making a wordplay joke at a suicide victim's funeral is very Larry Sanders. It fails in the room (as noted in the next beat), which is itself the point. Highly quotable. The show acknowledges the joke didn't work, which makes it funnier — Larry misjudges his audience, as always.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Really? What kind of car did Sid have?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: We... we never got to that.

jokes.text: 'No flipping.' / 'Shut up, Phil.'
jokes.setup: Larry delivers the 'whited out' joke at the funeral
jokes.punchline: Phil, apparently doing his cue card duties even at the funeral, instinctively calls 'No flipping' — then someone tells him to shut up
jokes.explanation: Pure situational genius: Phil's 'No flipping' is a show-production command that has leaked into real life — he's so conditioned by the show that he instinctively performs his job function at a funeral. The 'Shut up, Phil' is the perfect button. This is great absurdist character comedy from a minor character — the show's mundane institutional habits overriding the gravity of the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He had her stashed in a little place in the valley. He used to bang her at lunch.

jokes.text: 'That didn't go well. I shouldn't have done the whiting out joke.' / 'Oh, it was good.' / 'It didn't work, but you know why? Because you went so long.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie post-mortem the funeral speech as if it were a talk show segment
jokes.punchline: Both of them are critiquing the funeral performance using TV-production language — 'it didn't work because you went so long'
jokes.explanation: The note session after the funeral speech — treating it as a segment note rather than a human moment — is the episode's thesis statement in miniature. Artie giving Larry a note about his eulogy ('you went so long, you killed the audience') is among the most perfectly Larry-Sanders-show things that could happen.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I thought his wife was dead. Sid. No. I guess he liked to tell people that.

jokes.text: 'Should I go again?' — Larry considers re-delivering the eulogy
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie agree the funeral speech didn't land well
jokes.punchline: Larry sincerely asks if he should go back up for another try — treating the funeral like a do-over opportunity
jokes.explanation: Three words that are somehow one of the episode's biggest laughs. 'Should I go again?' — said sincerely, about a funeral eulogy — is the perfect crystallization of Larry's inability to distinguish between professional performance and human reality. The question implies he sees the funeral crowd as an audience to win back. Exceptional character integration and economy: three words do the work of a paragraph.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I guess he liked to tell people that.

jokes.text: Artie's single-word response: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks 'Should I go again?' about the funeral eulogy
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'No' — no elaboration, no explanation — is the appropriate response to an insane question delivered as though it's a reasonable one
jokes.explanation: A single word that contains multitudes. Artie doesn't justify it, doesn't elaborate — the question doesn't deserve elaboration. Maximum economy (10.0 — it's literally one word). The pause before it (implied) and the finality are what make it work. Rip Torn's delivery would be everything.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Can you imagine killing yourself over a couple of chicks?

jokes.text: 'I can't believe Larry actually showed up.' — reaction beat from a mourner at the funeral
jokes.setup: Larry has just delivered a self-promotional eulogy full of talk-show language at Sid's funeral
jokes.punchline: A mourner's reaction focuses not on the quality of the speech but on the surprise of Larry's mere presence
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character joke: Larry's reputation for not showing up for people is so entrenched that his physical presence at a funeral is remarkable. Underscores the Larry-Sanders-as-social-ghost theme without over-explaining it.

dialogue.speaker: Char the psychic
dialogue.line: He... he wants you to do the sketch.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe Larry actually showed up.'
jokes.setup: A reaction shot (or overheard line) from a funeral attendee after Larry's spectacularly inappropriate eulogy.
jokes.punchline: The disbelief isn't about the eulogy content — it's simply that Larry showed up at all, suggesting his reputation for avoidance is so well-known that physical presence is itself remarkable.
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective character-commentary beat. The joke is in the low bar — simply attending is remarkable — which says everything about Larry's reputation without needing to elaborate.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We'll have you on another night.

dialogue.speaker: Laura Dern
dialogue.line: No, you won't.

jokes.text: Larry meets Sid's brother Fred. Insists Sid was 'a very gifted actor who people laughed with and not at.'
jokes.setup: Larry introduces himself to Sid's brother and eulogizes Sid privately.
jokes.punchline: 'A very gifted actor who people laughed with and not at' — Larry directly echoes the exact phrase he reportedly used to destroy Sid ('you don't know the difference between being laughed with and being laughed at'), now desperately inverting it as if to undo the damage.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Larry's private verbal attack on Sid — 'you don't know the difference between being laughed with and being laughed at' — is now used verbatim in the inverted form as a tribute. He is literally trying to take back the words that he believes killed Sid by replacing them with their opposite. The structural craftsmanship here is exceptional: setup (id 10), development (Larry's guilt spiral), payoff (this callback). The comedy and tragedy are completely fused. This is what the best Larry Sanders writing looks like. Genuinely earns a 9.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I would love to cook for you, and... and, um... why don't we take a break?

jokes.text: 'He said you always ragged on him.' / 'I don't recall that.' / 'Um, there was some verbal sparring, of course. All in good fun. Um, you know, snaps.'
jokes.setup: Sid's brother tells Larry that Sid complained Larry always gave him a hard time
jokes.punchline: Larry's denial ('I don't recall that'), then gradual concession ('verbal sparring... all in good fun... snaps') — each step a tiny retreat from the lie
jokes.explanation: Larry's step-by-step retreat from denial — each word a calibrated capitulation — is a masterclass in cringe comedy. 'Snaps' as the final word is perfect: it's the least formal, most self-damning word he could choose. The escalating specificity of his backpedaling is finely observed and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Give my best to your mom and your dad, dern old bruce.

jokes.text: 'I'll take care of everything. The funeral, the bills, I'll take care of it.' / 'Why?' / '...because I loved him.'
jokes.setup: Fred mentions Sid left unpaid bills and insurance problems; Larry immediately offers to cover everything
jokes.punchline: Fred's baffled 'Why?' exposes that Larry's generosity is inexplicable — then Larry's long pause before '...because I loved him' plays as both true and as guilt-money
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'because I loved him' is where the whole episode lives. It's genuine AND it's guilt AND it's performative AND it's the closest Larry can get to taking responsibility. The structure — impulsive generosity, baffled question, long pause, simple answer — is beautifully calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It was like when you were interviewing Dan rather.

jokes.text: Rosie Grier prays at the funeral while Larry is simultaneously being introduced to Laura Dern by a producer — cutting between the prayer and the meeting
jokes.setup: Rosie Grier delivers a heartfelt funeral prayer: 'Father, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob...'
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts mid-prayer to Larry being introduced to a celebrity guest — the sacred and the showbiz occupying the same moment
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Rosie Grier's prayer and the show-booking mechanics happening simultaneously at the funeral is a structural joke that doesn't need a punchline — the collision is the joke. The show trusting this to land without underlining it is a sign of confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Aw, screw you, Larry. I gotta tell you something. My mom and I always hated you.

jokes.text: 'Wasn't it at a function where I don't remember you?'
jokes.setup: Larry and Laura are pretending they've never properly met, even though they're secretly dating
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'at a function where I don't remember you' — framing their non-memory as a shared event — is both truthful and inadvertently insulting
jokes.explanation: Beautifully awkward. Larry's phrasing — 'a function where I don't remember you' — is somehow both an honest admission and a bizarre insult to someone he's currently dating secretly. The phrase is syntactically strange in a way that feels entirely natural for the character. High economy and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, at you, but hilarious. You were good.

jokes.text: 'This is better.' — The producer's satisfied conclusion after watching Larry and Laura pretend not to know each other
jokes.setup: Larry and Laura do an awkward fake-first-meeting while secretly dating
jokes.punchline: The producer calls it 'better' — approvingly — as if this absurd performance of not-knowing each other is good television prep
jokes.explanation: Small but precise: the producer's 'This is better' affirms the performance they're all complicit in. The institutional approval of a lie is a recurring Larry Sanders theme delivered here in two words.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Were they, uh... were they laughing with me or were they laughing at me?

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Well, at you, but hilarious.

jokes.text: Artie introduces Heidi Klum as the 1998 Sports Illustrated swimsuit cover girl to Larry mid-conversation
jokes.setup: Larry is already talking to Laura Dern when Artie arrives with a supermodel
jokes.punchline: The awkward three-way introduction — Larry sandwiched between his secret girlfriend and a supermodel — is a cringe triangle that the show lets breathe
jokes.explanation: Social comedy of Larry caught between two women he can't openly acknowledge his relationship to either of — the cringe is situational rather than verbal. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, Sid, you fuck. You tricked me, buddy.

jokes.text: 'Don't forget the discover card.' / 'Oh, $2,400. Fuck me.' / 'Does anybody take discover anymore?'
jokes.setup: They're going through Sid's estate bills
jokes.punchline: Larry's concern pivots from the amount to the brand — 'Does anybody take Discover anymore?' — treating Sid's financial crisis as a consumer trend question
jokes.explanation: Larry's reaction to a dead man's debt is to worry about whether Discover Card is still relevant — a pitch-perfect exposure of his celebrity-class obliviousness. The 'Fuck me' lands as genuine, then the Discover observation makes it absurd. Very quotable, very specific to the character and the era.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Stiller
dialogue.line: I just ran into a psychic in the parking lot who told me that you and Laura are an item. Is this the truth? Is this the truth?

jokes.text: 'I could never fill those shoes.' — Hank refuses the Liza sketch, claiming loyalty to Sid
jokes.setup: They want Hank to do the Liza Minnelli sketch now that Sid is dead
jokes.punchline: Hank claims sentimental loyalty ('that's Sid's baby, I could never fill those shoes') — when he and Sid despised each other
jokes.explanation: Hank's cynical sentimentality is funny because it's so transparent — he's performing mourning for professional cover. The audience knows (from the Liza sketch fight earlier) that this is completely false.

jokes.text: 'What are all these warm, squishy, fuzzies for Sid all of a sudden? Don't shit me. You and Sid hated each other. Now you're mourning him like you're Yoko Ono.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been performing grief over Sid
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'warm, squishy fuzzies' + 'like you're Yoko Ono' — the Yoko reference implying Hank is performing grief for someone he helped destroy
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Yoko Ono' comparison is exceptional: it implies Hank is grieving something he destroyed, invoking the cultural mythology of Yoko as the figure who was present at a legend's end. 'Warm, squishy fuzzies' is a perfectly Artie-ish phrase — sentimental, contemptuous, and slightly absurd. The combination is very strong.

jokes.text: 'What kind of car did Sid have?' / 'We... we never got to that.'
jokes.setup: Hank claims his last conversation with Sid was about cars; Artie tests him
jokes.punchline: 'We never got to that' — Hank can't even name the type of car in his own alibi, exposing the lie completely
jokes.explanation: The trap-question and its perfect failure: Artie asks the simplest follow-up and Hank can't answer it. 'We never got to that' is the most damning possible response, equivalent to a confession. The setup is just one question; the punchline is five words. Exceptional economy and structure. The pause implied between Artie's question and Hank's response (indicated by timestamp gap at 14:34-14:48) makes this even better.

jokes.text: 'I'm a bad boy.' — Artie to the psychic, redirecting her from the office
jokes.setup: Char the psychic has just picked up on Larry's relationship with Laura; Artie needs to get her out
jokes.punchline: Artie's flirtatious 'If you can read my mind, you know that I'm a bad boy' — both charming her out of the room and hinting at genuine libertine self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Artie using flattery and self-deprecating charm as a crisis-management tool is very character-appropriate. 'Bad boy' is funny because it's both true (his libertine past) and completely absurd as a self-description for a 60s-something TV producer.

jokes.text: 'I'm not dating anyone.' / 'L-a, like Laura?' / 'Dern?'
jokes.setup: Char is doing letter-readings; Larry denies dating anyone
jokes.punchline: Char gets 'L-A' and Larry — trying to be unhelpful — supplies 'Dern?' completing the answer himself
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is perfect: Larry tries to derail the psychic by staying silent, but when she gets 'L-A' he can't help himself — 'Dern?' — completing the exposure he was trying to prevent. His inability to stop himself from helping is the punchline. Very character-specific: Larry's compulsive need to be helpful/correct overrides his self-interest.

jokes.text: 'Oh, what a relief! God, that explains why you weren't making a move on that Sports Illustrated babe.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just confirmed he's dating Laura Dern
jokes.punchline: Artie's relief is not about Larry's personal happiness — it's that Artie now understands why Larry wasn't pursuing Heidi Klum, which had apparently been bothering him
jokes.explanation: Artie's priorities are perfectly revealed: his relief is pragmatic, almost managerial — he's been wondering why Larry wasn't working the room properly. The implicit assumption that Larry should have been 'making a move' on Heidi Klum reveals Artie's old-school TV-producer worldview. Rip Torn's delivery would be golden.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, that's why Janice left him.' / 'Who's Janice?' / 'His wife.' / 'I thought his wife was dead.' / 'No.' / 'I guess he liked to tell people that.'
jokes.setup: Artie has revealed Sid had a secret girlfriend (Shirley); now reveals Sid has a living wife (Janice) who left him
jokes.punchline: Larry thought Sid's wife was dead — apparently Sid told people this. 'I guess he liked to tell people that.' The revelation that Sid fabricated his wife's death is darkly absurd.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's escalation peak for the Sid-revelation sequence. The reveal that Sid's 'dead wife' was alive and had simply left him — and that Sid told people she was dead — is the darkest and funniest detail in the episode. 'I guess he liked to tell people that' is delivered with perfect Artie nonchalance, as if people frequently do this. The specificity of Sid's pathology (killing off an estranged wife as a story) recontextualizes everything and is wickedly funny.

jokes.text: 'What a piece of work. Can you imagine killing yourself over a couple of chicks?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just learned the full scope of Sid's secret romantic life
jokes.punchline: Larry's summary — 'killing yourself over a couple of chicks' — reduces Sid's apparent psychological crisis to a casual bro-assessment, revealing Larry's emotional shallowness
jokes.explanation: Larry's casual framing of a suicide as being 'over a couple of chicks' is both revealing and darkly funny. The comedy is in the gap between the gravity of what happened and the register Larry processes it in.

jokes.text: Char the psychic wandering into the green room: 'There is no sprite in there.'
jokes.setup: Char has been bumped and is wandering the backstage area
jokes.punchline: Her first utterance is a mundane refrigerator complaint — 'there is no Sprite in there' — the most un-psychic thing a psychic could say
jokes.explanation: The joke is the total deflation of the psychic's mystique: she's wandering the green room complaining about the snack situation. The mundanity ('no Sprite') versus the mystical pretense she's been maintaining is a clean and efficient comedic contrast.

jokes.text: Char tells Hank she senses someone close to him with an 'S-I': 'Like a Sid or a Sidney?' / 'No. Nothing. I mean, nothing.' / 'He wants you to do the sketch.'
jokes.setup: Char is doing a cold reading on Hank; she picks up on an 'S-I' energy from a deceased person
jokes.punchline: She says Sid 'wants him to do the sketch' — as if Sid's ghost is sending messages through a psychic about a Liza Minnelli impression
jokes.explanation: The callback is excellent: the whole episode, Hank has been refusing to do the Liza sketch out of fake sentimentality. Now Sid's 'ghost' is being used to pressure him into doing it. The absurdism of a psychic relaying posthumous sketch notes is very funny, and Hank's 'No. Nothing. I mean, nothing' escalating denial is perfect Hank panic.

jokes.text: 'She travels alone? That's my instinct. Yeah, picked it up like that.' — Artie immediately claims psychic credit for confirming Laura Dern travels alone
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are doing a pre-interview with Laura Dern; Artie guesses she travels alone
jokes.punchline: Artie performs the same confidence a psychic has — 'picked it up like that' — having just spent the whole episode skeptical of the psychic
jokes.explanation: Artie doing the psychic's 'instinct' act right after spending the episode debunking psychics is a nice character irony. His self-satisfaction ('picked it up like that') mirrors Char's manner exactly.

jokes.text: Larry invites Laura Dern to his house in Cabo San Lucas mid-interview — while she's a guest he's supposed to interview about Mexico
jokes.setup: Larry mentions he has a place in Cabo; Laura confirms she loves traveling alone
jokes.punchline: Larry, barely disguising his personal interest, invites her to his house and offers to cook for her — on camera, on the show, in front of the crew
jokes.explanation: The horror of watching Larry awkwardly court his secret girlfriend on his own show — offering to cook for her, mentioning his house — while trying to maintain the fiction that they're strangers. The cringe of 'I would love to cook for you' on live television, to a woman he's secretly dating, is very Larry.

jokes.text: 'I sort of put a little tilde on that. Didn't I? Yes. We all do when we speak foreign languages.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just said 'Cabo San Lucas' with exaggerated Spanish pronunciation on air while trying to impress Laura.
jokes.punchline: 'We all do when we speak foreign languages' — Larry's self-satisfied generalization about a thing only he does, and that he's doing poorly.
jokes.explanation: 'We all do when we speak foreign languages' is a beautifully constructed piece of Larry-specific delusion — he's done something awkward and immediately universalized it as normal human behavior. The false authority in 'we all do' is very Larry. Quotable as a standalone line.

jokes.text: 'Why don't we take a break? And we'll be back with more of Laura Dern. No flipping.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just awkwardly offered his Cabo house to his secret girlfriend on live television
jokes.punchline: The 'No flipping' cue card command appears at the end of a deeply personal, awkward interview moment — Phil is still doing his job robotically through all of this
jokes.explanation: The 'No flipping' running gag continues — here it's funny because the card instruction is the only thing normal about the preceding few minutes of television. The show's mechanical rhythms persisting through personal chaos is the joke.

jokes.text: 'Give my best to your mom and your dad, dern old Bruce.' — Artie's farewell to Laura Dern
jokes.setup: Laura Dern is leaving after the interview
jokes.punchline: 'Dern old Bruce' — Artie uses her last name as an adjective, a mild wordplay pun on 'darned old Bruce' (Bruce Dern, her father)
jokes.explanation: A clever celebrity-insider pun: 'dern old Bruce' uses Dern as an expletive substitute (like 'darned') while naming her actual father (Bruce Dern). Very Artie — old-school Hollywood, warm but cleverly executed. Rewards industry knowledge.

jokes.text: 'I don't think they could tell there was any underlying sexual chemistry, do you?' / 'None at all. No.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie debrief after the Laura Dern interview, in which Larry awkwardly flirted with his secret girlfriend on live TV
jokes.punchline: Larry asks if the 'underlying sexual chemistry' was visible; Artie says 'None at all' — both lying or deluded
jokes.explanation: Larry's inability to read his own performance — asking for confirmation that the most obvious thing was invisible — and Artie's enabling 'none at all' is a perfect encapsulation of their dynamic. The phrase 'underlying sexual chemistry' in Artie's mouth would be funny regardless of context.

jokes.text: Liza Minnelli comes out a SECOND time and launches into 'Cabaret' again — live on air
jokes.setup: The episode has already shown us the Liza sketch in rehearsal, where she couldn't be stopped
jokes.punchline: The live version of the Liza bit plays out — the audience now knows what's coming, and the replay of the unstoppable Liza dynamic is the joke
jokes.explanation: The live-show version of the Liza sketch works because we've seen the rehearsal — we know she can't be stopped, and watching it happen again on air is funnier for the expectation. The structural payoff of the episode-opening rehearsal is earned here.

jokes.text: 'Aw, screw you, Larry.' / 'I gotta tell you something. My mom and I always hated you.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to cut off Liza mid-song during the live broadcast, as rehearsed
jokes.punchline: Liza delivers the 'Screw you / my mom and I always hated you' line — which we heard in rehearsal — but it lands even harder live, with the Judy Garland implication now settled as a recurring Liza character bit
jokes.explanation: The live-show delivery of the 'My mom and I always hated you' line hits harder than the rehearsal for several reasons: (1) it's happening on air, (2) the audience at home and in-show get it simultaneously, (3) we've been primed by the rehearsal to anticipate it, making the structure tighter. The Judy Garland subtext has calcified into a real joke by now. This is the episode's single biggest laugh, combining callback, escalation, and character specificity at the highest level. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: 'Were they laughing with me or were they laughing at me?' / 'Well, at you, but hilarious.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just done the Liza Minnelli sketch — the very thing he claimed he could never do because it was Sid's 'baby'
jokes.punchline: Hank asks the exact question that the episode's theme has circled around (laughed with vs. laughed at) and gets an answer: laughed at, but successfully so
jokes.explanation: The episode's thematic payoff joke. This phrase — 'laughed with vs. laughed at' — was introduced as a weapon used against Hank (03:40), then weaponized by Larry against Sid (implied to have contributed to his death), and now Hank sincerely asks it about himself after doing the sketch Sid died before doing. Larry's answer ('At you, but hilarious') redeems the phrase by suggesting that being laughed at isn't a death sentence — it's still comedy. The episode's entire emotional arc is compressed into this exchange. The craft is exceptional because the joke is structurally the culmination of a thematic thread, not a standalone gag.

jokes.text: 'Oh, Sid, you fuck. You tricked me, buddy.'
jokes.setup: The Liza sketch worked — Hank pulled it off
jokes.punchline: Larry's private address to Sid — 'you tricked me' — implies Sid's death forced the sketch to happen and somehow worked out; the profanity of 'you fuck' aimed at a dead man is both funny and genuinely moving
jokes.explanation: The episode's most emotionally resonant joke — comedy and grief in perfect balance. 'Oh, Sid, you fuck' is simultaneously an insult, an endearment, a eulogy, and an absolution. It's Larry's version of grief: profane, private, and routed through the show. 'You tricked me, buddy' completes it — Sid's death forced Larry to feel something genuine. The economy is extraordinary (eight words), the character integration is total (only Larry Sanders speaks this way), and it rewards every rewatch. Among the best moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Jerry Stiller immediately pivots from small talk to: 'I just ran into a psychic in the parking lot who told me you and Laura are an item. Is this the truth?'
jokes.setup: Larry has been desperately protecting his secret relationship with Laura Dern all episode; Jerry Stiller is a late guest
jokes.punchline: The psychic Larry had bumped to protect the secret immediately told the secret to the next guest in the parking lot — the information escaped anyway
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing callback: every effort Larry made to contain the secret has failed spectacularly — the psychic he bumped went straight to the parking lot and told the next guest. The irony that bumping her from the show only moved the revelation to an uncontrolled location is structurally beautiful. Jerry Stiller asking 'Is this the truth?' on live television is the nightmare scenario Larry spent the whole episode trying to prevent. This is precision plotting as comedy — the joke is the architecture of the plot itself.

jokes.text: Larry introduces Jerry Stiller as 'George's father on Seinfeld' and notes 'Seinfeld is going off the air, but you have a whole career happening, don't you?' / Stiller: 'There's a life after Seinfeld, but forget about my life. What about your life?'
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the substitute guest (Jerry Stiller replaced the psychic) and awkwardly references Seinfeld ending.
jokes.punchline: Stiller pivots immediately back to Larry's situation — 'forget about my life, what about your life?' — given that Larry's show is also ending, the irony is pointed.
jokes.explanation: A nice meta layer — two shows ending simultaneously, with the guest redirecting the host to his own mortality. The real-world resonance (Larry Sanders was also in its final season in 1998, same as Seinfeld) adds a documentary quality. Stiller's pivot is sharp.

tmdb_overview: Everyone takes Sid's death hard, especially Hank who thinks he may have pushed Sid over the edge.
